title: CIMC study monitoring dashboard
text:
0.1 Recruitment monitoring
Data are current through 24 August 2026. This front page is operational: it shows recruitment flow, survey completion, and participants requiring action.
Current source. Linked dummy development data; staged at 2026-09-14 18:04:13 UTC. Change source.mode in dashboard.yml to switch between development and production ingestion.
What. This page gives the study team a current operational picture of recruitment, enrollment, follow-up and missing reports. It covers the client-specified recruitment trajectory, screening funnel, site delivery, daily completion trend, follow-up queue, recent participant tracking, and site completion.
How. Records are linked by participant ID. Expected reports run from enrollment to the earliest of the configured follow-up end, data cutoff, or recorded method stop. The action lists apply the thresholds documented in dashboard.yml.
Why. It supports day-to-day decisions: whether recruitment is on target, whether follow-up is being sustained, and which participants may need timely contact. It is a monitoring page, not a clinical outcomes analysis.

0.1.1 Cumulative enrollment
What it shows. Actual cumulative enrollment against the straight-line plan implied by the configured recruitment start date, target date, and site targets.
How it is calculated. Enrollments are counted once on their enrollment date. The planned line rises evenly from zero to the total configured target; it is a monitoring reference rather than a statistical model.











0.1.2 Recruitment funnel
What it shows. Unique people at successive stages from screening through daily reporting and completion of the observation window.
How it is calculated. A person appears in every stage they have reached, so this is a cumulative funnel rather than a set of mutually exclusive groups.
Why it helps. The largest drop between adjacent stages identifies where recruitment or onboarding may need attention.











0.1.3 Enrollment against site targets
What it shows. Enrollment achieved at each site relative to its configured target.
How it is calculated. Enrolled participants are counted once at their enrollment site and divided by that site’s target in dashboard.yml.
Why it helps. It distinguishes overall recruitment success from site-specific delivery. It does not measure reporting quality after enrollment.

0.2.1 Participant progress
What it shows. The current follow-up status of enrolled participants within each site.
How it is calculated. Status uses the configured observation window and method-discontinuation responses. “Reached day 90” means the time window elapsed; it does not require perfect questionnaire completion.
Why it helps. It separates participants who remain under active follow-up from those who have completed, stopped, or never begun daily reporting.











0.2.2 Daily completion trend
What it shows. The proportion of expected daily reports actually received in each site-week.
How it is calculated. Each point divides received participant-days by expected participant-days among people under observation that week.
Why it helps. It separates growth in the enrolled cohort from genuine reporting adherence and makes site-specific implementation changes visible over time.











0.2.3 Completion by site











Daily participant tracking — most recent 14 days

What it shows. A compact recent completion calendar for the active participants most in need of attention. Green cells are received daily forms, coral cells are missed due forms, and grey cells were not due.
How it is calculated. Rows prioritise participants meeting the consecutive-miss rule and then those with the lowest overall daily completion. The number of displayed rows and days is configurable. Participant identifiers are shown only when publication of action lists is enabled.












Monthly participant tracking — all study months

What it shows. One cell per participant and calendar month since recruitment began, separated by study site. Purple indicates a received monthly section and amber indicates a section that was due but missing.
How it is calculated. Monthly due dates use the configured day of month and each participant’s observed follow-up interval. Rows with the most missing monthly sections appear first within each site.

title: CIMC study monitoring dashboard
text:
0.3 Potential protocol deviations and violations
What it shows. This section screens linked study forms for records that may represent a protocol deviation or violation. The supplied rules include CIMC reports without enrollment, missing programme start dates, reports dated before enrollment, duplicate participant-days, duplicate enrollments, and enrollments without recruitment records.
How it is calculated. Exact participant IDs and recorded dates are compared across recruitment, enrollment, and CIMC submissions. Each rule and its provisional classification are controlled in dashboard.yml. CIMC submissions without a valid linked programme start remain in this monitoring register but are excluded from symptom and cycle analyses.
Why it helps. A linkage problem should create an actionable signal rather than prevent the dashboard from rendering. These are potential events: the dashboard does not determine seriousness, causality, or reportability. The study team must verify source records and adjudicate each flag under the approved protocol and deviation-management procedures.

text:
0.5 Completion-pattern UpSet chart
What it shows. Exact combinations of reporting and follow-up milestones reached by participants.
How it is calculated. The upper bars count participants in each combination; filled dots identify the milestones included in that combination.
Why it helps. It shows whether apparent progress is driven by complete follow-up, strong daily adherence, monthly completion, or only one of those elements.

title: CIMC study monitoring dashboard
text:
0.7 Monitoring definitions

Expected daily reports run from enrollment through the earliest of the configured follow-up day (90), the data cutoff, or a recorded method stop date.
Monthly reports expected are calendar-month sections due on configured day 1 of a month within that observed interval. The supplied setting matches the revised CIMC form.
Current consecutive missed days count backwards from the participant’s latest due day. A submitted form breaks the streak.
Reached day 90 describes elapsed follow-up time, not questionnaire adherence.
All thresholds and site targets are editable in dashboard.yml.

title: 2  Study profile and demographics
text:
2.1 Age distribution
This page describes the people who completed the enrollment and sociodemographic form. Percentages use enrolled participants as their denominator unless a site-specific denominator is shown. These are descriptive distributions, not evidence that recruitment is representative of a wider population.
What. This page describes who has enrolled, including age, education, contraceptive method, relationship status and reminder preferences.
How. Each enrolled participant contributes one record. Site panels retain site-specific wording where the forms are not directly equivalent, while a small number of clearly defined variables are harmonised for comparison.
Why. The distributions help the team understand the cohort being followed, identify site imbalances, and judge how cautiously pooled study-level summaries should be interpreted.
What it shows. The first chart preserves exact age; the second groups ages to compare site composition.
How it is calculated. Age-group boundaries and labels come from dashboard.yml, and every enrolled participant remains in the denominator.
Why it helps. It shows both the detailed age distribution and whether sites are enrolling meaningfully different age profiles.

title: 2  Study profile and demographics
text:
2.2 Education
What it shows. Education responses within each site.
How it is calculated. Categories are retained exactly because the three site versions differ, and percentages use enrolled participants at that site.
Why it helps. It describes the cohort without forcing unlike qualifications into a potentially misleading common hierarchy.

title: 2  Study profile and demographics
text:
2.3 Contraceptive method at enrollment
What it shows. The contraceptive methods represented within each study site.
How it is calculated. Each participant is counted once using the method recorded at enrollment.
Why it helps. Method mix may influence bleeding and pain patterns, so large site differences matter when interpreting pooled outcomes.

title: 2  Study profile and demographics
section: 2.4 Time since contraceptive initiation at enrollment
text:
2.4 Time since contraceptive initiation at enrollment
What it shows. How recently the contraceptive was initiated when each participant enrolled.
How it is calculated. The recorded start date is subtracted from enrollment date and grouped using configured time bands.
Why it helps. Follow-up experiences may differ by time since initiation, and the chart also exposes records outside the configured 74-day eligibility window.

title: 2  Study profile and demographics
text:
2.5 Partner status
The forms use different site-specific wording. For monitoring only, responses are harmonised into broad living-arrangement categories; the original response fields remain available in the source CSV.

title: 2  Study profile and demographics
text:
2.6 Reminder preferences
Because daily reminders permit multiple selections, combinations are shown as reported rather than split into percentages that would exceed 100%.

title: 2  Study profile and demographics
text:
2.7 Recruitment exclusions
This final distribution is based on screened people who were not eligible. Reasons are mutually exclusive in the dummy data so totals can be interpreted directly; a production export may require a prespecified hierarchy when several criteria fail.

title: 2  Study profile and demographics
text:
2.8 Interpretation notes

Demographic charts use one row per enrolled participant.
Site-specific education and partner questions are not assumed to be perfectly equivalent.
“No response” is retained rather than silently excluded from denominators.
The dummy data are designed to exercise the dashboard and do not represent expected study prevalence.

title: 3  Wits MRU monitoring
text:
3.1 Site action lists
Data are current through 24 August 2026. This page is restricted to Wits MRU and uses the same study-wide configuration, denominators, and alert rules as the central dashboard.
What it does. It brings recruitment, daily and monthly completion, individual reporting patterns, follow-up queues, expandable action lists, and data-quality checks into one operational site view.
Why it helps. Site teams can identify and manage their own follow-up problems without filtering the central dashboard or receiving records belonging to another site.
These are operational participant-level worklists for this site. The expandable tables are intended to make the reason for each flag and the expected follow-up clear without requiring a CSV download. The CSV files continue to be generated and routed separately for operational use and audit. In a downloaded Kobo dashboard archive, the site CSVs are stored in the actions/ folder; they are not part of the rendered website itself. When action-list publication is enabled, the same records can also be inspected in the expandable tables below.

Data are current through 24 August 2026. This page is restricted to Profamilia and uses the same study-wide configuration, denominators, and alert rules as the central dashboard.
What it does. It brings recruitment, daily and monthly completion, individual reporting patterns, follow-up queues, expandable action lists, and data-quality checks into one operational site view.
Why it helps. Site teams can identify and manage their own follow-up problems without filtering the central dashboard or receiving records belonging to another site.
These are operational participant-level worklists for this site. The expandable tables are intended to make the reason for each flag and the expected follow-up clear without requiring a CSV download. The CSV files continue to be generated and routed separately for operational use and audit. In a downloaded Kobo dashboard archive, the site CSVs are stored in the actions/ folder; they are not part of the rendered website itself. When action-list publication is enabled, the same records can also be inspected in the expandable tables below.

title: 5  OHSU monitoring
text:
5.1 Site action lists
Data are current through 24 August 2026. This page is restricted to OHSU and uses the same study-wide configuration, denominators, and alert rules as the central dashboard.
What it does. It brings recruitment, daily and monthly completion, individual reporting patterns, follow-up queues, expandable action lists, and data-quality checks into one operational site view.
Why it helps. Site teams can identify and manage their own follow-up problems without filtering the central dashboard or receiving records belonging to another site.
These are operational participant-level worklists for this site. The expandable tables are intended to make the reason for each flag and the expected follow-up clear without requiring a CSV download. The CSV files continue to be generated and routed separately for operational use and audit. In a downloaded Kobo dashboard archive, the site CSVs are stored in the actions/ folder; they are not part of the rendered website itself. When action-list publication is enabled, the same records can also be inspected in the expandable tables below.

title: 6  Daily bleeding and pain
text:
6.1 How to read this report
This report answers several related—but different—questions. Keeping the unit and denominator clear is essential because the same participant can submit many daily forms, several monthly forms, and observations from multiple menstrual cycles.
Confidence intervals. Whiskers on proportion bar charts are participant-clustered 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The bootstrap resamples whole participants—not individual rows—so all daily or monthly records from the same person remain together. Wider intervals mean the estimate is less precise. They describe sampling uncertainty in this dataset; they do not correct bias from missing reports, an unrepresentative sample, or a misspecified cycle rule.
Important interpretation boundary. These analyses are descriptive. A difference over time or between cycles is not, by itself, evidence that the contraceptive caused the difference. Formal causal questions would require a prespecified comparison design and statistical model.

text:
6.3 Daily questionnaire overview
The daily form records symptoms about the previous day. The dummy data contain repeated submissions from the same participants, so percentages below describe submissions rather than unique people unless stated otherwise.
What. This section describes bleeding and pain one day at a time.
How. Each submitted daily form is initially one observation. Conditional follow-up questions use only forms for which the question applied—for example, pain severity is calculated only among forms reporting pain.
Why. Daily reporting captures short-term variation that a monthly recall question may smooth over or forget. It is especially useful for identifying timing and symptom co-occurrence.

title: 6  Daily bleeding and pain
text:
6.4 Daily symptom trend
What it shows. The lines show the percentage of submitted daily forms reporting bleeding or pain on each calendar date.
How to read it. Peaks indicate dates on which a larger share of available submissions were positive. They do not necessarily mean more participants were enrolled on those dates, so completion volume and missingness should be checked alongside the trend.










6.4.1 Daily symptom prevalence by study site
What it shows. This selected site breakdown compares the proportion of daily submissions reporting bleeding or pain across the three study sites.
How it is calculated. The denominator is submitted daily forms within each site. Confidence intervals resample whole participants within that site, so repeated forms from one participant remain together.
Why it helps. A pooled percentage can conceal operational, population, or reporting differences between sites. The chart is descriptive and should prompt investigation rather than a causal conclusion about site.

title: 6  Daily bleeding and pain
text:
6.9 Time since contraceptive initiation
Elapsed time since programme_start_date is directly observed and does not depend on bleeding-pattern inference. The chart divides follow-up into consecutive 30-day programme periods. Within each period, each participant contributes once to each symptom percentage regardless of how many daily forms they submitted.
Why this view is useful. It asks whether the proportion of participants ever reporting bleeding or pain changes as exposure time accumulates, without requiring a menstrual cycle to be successfully inferred.

title: 6  Daily bleeding and pain
section: 6.10 Inferred menstrual cycles and cycle length
text:
6.10 Inferred menstrual cycles and cycle length
Cycle numbering is participant-specific and begins after programme_start_date, the contraceptive/programme start date. The first confirmed menstrual onset after that date is inferred cycle 1, followed by inferred cycle 2, cycle 3, and so on. With the supplied configuration, CD1 is the first non-spotting bleeding day followed by blood reported on the next consecutive calendar day. Confirmed onsets less than the configured minimum interval apart are not allowed to increment the inferred cycle number. Distinct shorter events remain bleeding episodes and can be analysed separately.
What is being inferred. The form does not contain an official cycle number or confirmed biological cycle start. The analysis therefore applies an explicit, configurable rule to observed bleeding reports.
Why this needs caution. Missing daily forms can hide an onset and make two true cycles appear as one long interval. Long intervals are retained and flagged rather than silently removed, so the team can review whether they reflect genuine bleeding patterns or incomplete observation.









The final observed cycle for each participant has no subsequent CD1 and is therefore right-censored; it is not included in the cycle-length chart. Intervals longer than the configurable review threshold are retained and highlighted: these may be genuine long intervals, or may indicate that an intervening onset was missed because the required daily reports were unavailable.

title: 6  Daily bleeding and pain
section: 6.12 Pain timing within successive inferred cycles
text:
6.12 Pain timing within successive inferred cycles
The heatmap retains actual cycle day rather than stretching every cycle to 28 days. Within each programme-cycle and cycle-day cell, each participant contributes at most once per region. The denominator is participants who submitted a daily report for that programme cycle and cycle day, so longer cycles and better reporters do not automatically contribute more weight to another cell.
What it shows. Darker cells indicate that a larger percentage of participants observed on that cycle day reported the body region.
Why it matters. The heatmap can reveal pain concentrated around inferred cycle onset, appearing later in the cycle, or recurring at similar times across successive cycles. It remains descriptive because cycle day is inferred from bleeding—not confirmed ovulation.









All symmetric regions are shown in one continuous heatmap. Vertical lines separate successive inferred cycles and the x-axis restarts at cycle day 1 within each section. Explicit zero-report cells remain visible; pale grey means there was no eligible participant report for that inferred cycle day, so a percentage cannot be calculated. Set bodymap.top_regions_timing to an integer in the config only if a shorter, highest-prevalence subset is wanted.

6.12.1 Cumulative pain-site burden within each inferred cycle
What it shows. This companion heatmap collapses the daily timing information into one value for each region and inferred cycle. A participant who reports a region on several days has a larger value than someone who reports it once.
How it is calculated. For each participant and completed inferred cycle, the numerator is observed daily forms on which the region was reported and the denominator is all observed daily forms in that cycle. These participant-level proportions are then averaged, giving every participant equal weight despite differences in form completion.
Why it matters. The ever-reported chart measures how widely a site occurs across participants. This measure instead captures persistence across days. A region can therefore have broad reach but low cumulative burden, or affect fewer participants repeatedly.









Rows are ordered by cumulative burden across the displayed cycles. A value of 10%, for example, means that the average participant reported that region on 10% of their observed daily forms within that completed cycle. This is a reporting-day burden measure rather than a biological duration estimate: unsubmitted days remain unknown.


6.12.2 Available participants by inferred cycle and cycle day
This retention-style chart shows the denominator behind the heatmap. Each line is an inferred cycle; its height on a given cycle day is the number of participants who supplied a daily report on that day. A falling line therefore reflects a mixture of shorter cycles and missing daily forms. It resembles an at-risk curve, but it is not a formal survival estimate because participants can miss one day and submit again later.









Cycle day is anchored to observed bleeding rather than biologically confirmed ovulation. Cycle lengths are not normalised: later days naturally have smaller denominators when fewer participants have cycles of that length or supplied a report on that day. Any local increase after a fall indicates renewed form submission, not participants re-entering a biological risk set.

title: 8  Technical appendix
text:
8.1 Configuring the dashboard
The dashboard’s study-specific settings are held in one file: dashboard.yml. This keeps choices such as study dates, site targets, reminder thresholds, cycle-inference rules, and display limits separate from the R analysis code.
What this means. Most routine adaptations should require a change to the configuration file followed by a fresh render—not edits scattered through the analysis pages.
Why it helps. Keeping assumptions in one clearly annotated file makes them easier to review with the study team, apply consistently across all pages, and record when the dashboard is updated.

title: 8  Technical appendix
text:
8.1.1 Safe editing workflow

Make a copy of the current dashboard.yml before making a substantial change.
Open the file in a plain-text editor and change only the value after the relevant colon.
Keep the existing indentation. YAML uses spaces to show which settings belong together; tabs should not be used.
Save the file, render the Quarto book again, and review the study-wide and relevant site data-quality sections as well as the chart affected by the change.
Record analytically important changes—especially cycle rules, denominators, date cutoffs, and confidence levels—so results from different dashboard versions are not compared as if their definitions were identical.

YAML values have a few conventions:

true and false turn options on or off.
null means no limit; for example, all pain regions are displayed.
Text can be quoted, and dates should remain quoted in YYYY-MM-DD form.
Proportions are written between 0 and 1, so 0.80 means 80%.
Lists use square brackets, for example [18, 24, 29, 34].

For example, this changes the missed-daily-report alert from three consecutive days to four:
monitoring:
  consecutive_missed_days: 4

The controlling setting is:

Use development while testing with the dummy datasets. For live Kobo data, enter the correct server and add all deployed asset UIDs to the three lists under data_source.production, store the API token in the environment variable named by api_token_environment_variable, and then change the mode to production.

      - "DAILY_ASSET_SITE_3"
All listed versions must use the same analysis field names. The preparation step downloads each asset, records its source UID in _dashboard_source_asset_uid, combines the rows, and only then runs the normal schema and linkage checks. Duplicate UIDs within a list are ignored to prevent accidental double counting.
The API token itself must not be written into dashboard.yml or committed to GitHub. Production action lists are also excluded from the rendered site by default because they can contain participant identifiers or contact information.
During early live testing, Kobo may omit a question from its JSON response when every downloaded submission skipped that question. The importer therefore treats unanswered monthly outcome fields as empty rather than assuming the connected asset is wrong. When a test record lacks the form’s calculated report date, it uses the calendar day before the Kobo submission timestamp because CIMC questions describe “yesterday.” If no monthly records are yet due, the monthly page displays a “not yet available” explanation and will populate after the first eligible monthly submission. Participant identifiers and the core CIMC routing fields are still validated so an incorrect asset UID or incompatible form does not pass silently.


8.1.4 Settings that change the meaning of results
Some settings affect presentation only, while others change the underlying calculation. Changes to the following should be agreed and documented before results are compared over time:

study.data_cutoff, follow-up duration, and monthly due-day rules;
participant ID, report-date, programme-start, or pain-location field mappings;
any setting under cycle_inference;
monitoring thresholds used to construct operational lists;
demographic boundaries or site definitions;
the confidence level and participant-bootstrap settings.

By contrast, chart titles, the number of intersections displayed, and the visible chart window generally change presentation rather than the source records. A shorter display window can still hide later observations from view, so it should be described clearly.


8.1.5 Rebuilding the dashboard
After saving the configuration, render the complete Quarto project from the project folder. The pre-render step prepares either the dummy or Kobo data, the R code recalculates every page, and the completed HTML book is written to docs/.
quarto render
Do not manually edit files inside docs/: they are generated outputs and will be replaced during the next render. If a render stops after a configuration change, first check spelling, indentation, quote pairing, and whether list labels and boundaries contain compatible numbers of entries.


8.1.6 What the dashboard is written in
All data preparation, statistical summaries, confidence intervals, tables, and plots are implemented in R. The report pages are Quarto documents (.qmd), while dashboard.yml supplies YAML settings. The published HTML also uses CSS for appearance and a small amount of JavaScript for interactive elements such as body-map hover labels. No Python analysis pipeline is used.

8.2 Technical appendix: detailed ever-reported pain location map
This version retains every original SVG region, including left/right and dorsal/ventral distinctions. Locations come only from pain-positive daily submissions; percentages use all unique participants as the denominator, and each participant contributes at most once per detailed region across the observation period.
What it answers. “Did this participant ever report pain in this exact anatomical region during follow-up?” Repeated reports in the same region do not increase that participant’s contribution.
Why it is in the appendix. The detailed map preserves laterality and body surface for clinical or instrument-development review, while the symmetric map earlier in the report provides the clearer primary summary.
